strengths: The paper addresses an important problem with a useful benchmark: user-level private federated ASR using a 255M-parameter transformer, naturally partitioned speech data, and realistic domain shifts between public pretraining and federated adaptation.

Per-layer clipping produces substantial empirical improvements at matched clipping bounds and noise levels. In Table 1, dimension-based clipping reduces English test WER from 31.1% to 20.4% at σ_DP = 3×10⁻⁶, demonstrating valuable robustness to injected noise.

The empirical study is extensive, covering initialization, cohort size, data heterogeneity, server optimizers, augmentation, local computation, and three languages. Transferring training configurations across languages provides useful evidence of recipe robustness.

Public datasets, detailed configurations, pseudocode, compute reporting, and a repository link support reproducibility. The manuscript explicitly labels extrapolated results and explains its public-seed assumptions; this transparency is valuable.
weaknesses: The central convergence claim has incompatible conditions. Corollary 1 requires κ = 1 − 8(1 − η_loc T_loc)² > 0, but prescribes η_loc = Θ(1/(L√(T_loc T))). For fixed local steps, η_loc T_loc approaches zero and κ approaches −7. Consequently, the claimed asymptotic convergence rate and recovery of prior bounds do not follow. Moreover, the displayed nonvanishing DP-noise term does not establish convergence to a stationary point.

There are additional substantive proof gaps. Equations (33)–(34) treat the LAMB preconditioner p_h^(t) as independent of the current DP noise, although Equations (10)–(15) compute it from that same noisy aggregate. The expectation factorization and cancellation of cross terms are therefore unjustified. Equation (20) also infers bounded sample gradients from smoothness without a stated bounded-domain or bounded-gradient assumption.

The headline privacy–utility combinations are not experimentally demonstrated. The relevant English runs use 34,753 users and cohorts of 1,024, with reported ε around 10⁷–10⁸. Obtaining ε = 4.5 or 7.2 requires extrapolation to approximately 7M or 70M users and cohorts of 204,800 while assuming preserved WER. Although disclosed, this assumption remains unvalidated; the nonprivate cohort-scaling experiments do not establish utility under the projected private training conditions.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed importance of combining LAMB with per-layer clipping under DP. Optimizer comparisons in Tables 8–9 are nonprivate, whereas the private experiments use LAMB throughout. Matched comparisons of clipping strategies across LAMB and Adam under noise are needed. Repeated-run uncertainty is also absent, making the small French/German gains difficult to assess. One architecture and model size provide limited support for broader claims about large models.

Privacy accounting and reporting need reconciliation. Algorithm 1 fixes cohort size in the implementation, whereas the stated accountant assumes independent Bernoulli sampling; the manuscript does not justify this substitution. Table 1 also reports ε = 1.3 and ε = 13 for identical accountant inputs z = 1.024, q ≈ 0.0295, T = 2,006, and δ = 10⁻⁹. These inconsistencies reduce confidence in a central claimed contribution.
